newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakh bankers back govt's $280 million debt plan.
newsitem.headline: Kazakh bankers back govt's $280 million debt plan.

text.p: Kazakh bankers gave a largely positive reaction to Prime Minister Akezhan Kazhegeldin's announcement on Tuesday that the former Soviet republic plans to borrow $280 million to help pay off debts to its pensioners.

Kazhegeldin told diplomats and journalists that Kazakhstan would raise by the end of the year $280 million on international markets and cut spending to pay off $500 million in state debts to pensioners.
"We are now on the road to cutting our budget expenses for 1997 -- this is $220 million. The rest of the money will be borrowed on international markets after receiving a new credit rating," he said.
The reaction to Kazhegeldin's words from local banks was quick and largely positive.

Murat Altynbayev, head of the dealing department at the state-run Bank TuranAlem, said: "It (future borrowing) is positive because another way out -- extra issues of money -- would be much more painful both for the population and the economy."
"We will have to pay anyway for this borrowing but it is cheaper. The question is where to get dollars to pay it off," Altynbayev said, adding that the government could cut financing of social items.

Aidan Karibzhanov, deputy managing director of Global Kazkommerts Securities, an investment branch of Kazkommertsbank, said: "This is good -- the government seeks renewed access to international money markets instead of raising taxes."
Kazakhstan issued a debut three-year $200 million Eurobond in December last year, priced to yield 9.3 percent or 350 basis points above comparable U.S. treasury notes.
Moody's gave Kazakhstan a Ba3 sovereign ceiling for long-term foreign currency bonds. Rating agencies IBCA and Standard and Poor's both gave Kazakhstan BB-.
National Bank of Kazakhstan Chairman Uraz Dzhandosov said earlier this month he expected a new credit rating by October, after which the republic would issue another dollar-denominated bond.
"On the one hand, such borrowings are cheaper. On the other hand, this is a chance to attract foreign investors to Kazakhstan," Karibzhanov said.

Korotay Turysov, chairman of the economy, finance and budget committee of the Mazhilis lower chamber of the Kazakh parliament, said a new borrowing on international markets was "a civilised method of resolving painful social issues".
He said the government was also expected to present to the legislature a revised version of Kazakhstan's budget by May 15, sequestering, or cutting, some planned spending.
"Some money to cover in part pension arrears still can be found in the budget by sequestering some of its articles," said Turysov but gave no details.
